newsitem.title: USA: Apache tests two zones of Qarun discovery.
newsitem.headline: Apache tests two zones of Qarun discovery.

text.p: Apache Corp said on Tuesday an oil discovery on its Qarun Concession in Egypt's Western Desert tested at a combined rate of 3,700 barrels of oil per day from two separate formations, the Kharita and the Lower Bahariya.

Testing of these zones in the SW Qarun-1X (formerly the C-1X/Sakr) well continues, while additional indicated pay zones in the Lower and Upper Bahariya will be tested at a later date. The new field will be known as SW Qarun.
Apache owns 75 percent of the contractor interest in the Qarun Concession, while Global Natural Resources Inc owns the remaining 25 percent.
The concession is operated by Qarun Petroleum Co and owned jointly by the contractors and the national oil company.

As scheduled, Apache said, oil from the Concession began flowing into permanent production facilities last week and is now being transported through a pipeline to two 350,000-barrel storage tanks, located about 30 miles to the east.
It said sales should begin in November once the tanks are filled. The SW Qarun field discovery is expected to be connected to this pipeline in a matter of weeks.
Qarun field has been producing since November 1995 under an early production arrangement whereby the oil has been transported by truck to a local refinery.

Apache said oil production is now averaging 16,000 barrels per day and is expected to increase to an estimated 40,000 barrels per day by year end as additional field wells, along with the new field discovery, are tied to the existing production facilities and pipeline.

The Kharita zone in the new well flowed at a daily rate of 2,600 barrels of 40 degree gravity oil. It was tested on a one-inch choke with 58 pounds per square inch of flowing tubing pressure from perforations between 9,933 feet and 9,953 feet.

The Lower Bahariya zone flowed at a daily rate of 1,100 barrels of 36 degree gravity oil. It was tested on a one-inch choke with a flowing tubing pressure of 44 pounds per square inch. Perforations were between 9,160 feet and 9,350 feet.
